newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar in doldrums, up slightly in late Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Dollar in doldrums, up slightly in late Tokyo.

text.p: The dollar was holding steady in dull late Tokyo trade Wednesday as the market searched for direction, with little immediate impact from a much-awaited news conference by Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka.
The greenback remained mired in a 115.00-115.55 yen range, its downside supported by investor bids. It lacked the energy to rise above early offers placed near 115.60 yen.

Sharp falls in Japanese stocks, which saw the benchmark Nikkei 225 average shed 215.81 points or 1.14 percent to close at 18,680.38, supported the greenback, and even helped it climb slightly in mid-afternoon trade. But dealers said the impact of stocks' weakness was diminishing as a factor.

"Certainly these falls in the Nikkei, combined with the strength of U.S. stocks, is making it easier to sell yen, but the connection between the Nikkei and the yen appears to be weakening a bit," one city bank dealer said.
Bids were placed near 115.00-115.10 yen, probably from trust banks.
Additional bids were likely from importers at the upper end of the 114-yen level, a local bank dealer said.

But dealers said the volume of these was small at best, and noted that a downside risk remains. The city bank dealer said there appeared to be some options with a strike price from 114.30 to 114.80 yen, meaning that further sales could be triggered should the dollar slide to that level.

The topside remained heavy after offers emerged from U.S. fund operators at around 115.60 yen in morning trade. There were vague rumours of sales near this level by an Asian central bank, but these could not be confirmed, dealers said.
"U.S. funds appeared to be taking some quick profits, as there are few signs of the dollar rising as far as 116 yen anytime soon," a city bank dealer said.

But the overall mood of the market was apathetic, with operators looking forward to the release of key U.S. indicators, such as December Producer Price Index (PPI) and employment data, later this week.

"There's also a big question in everyone's mind about the attitude of the U.S. government towards the dollar's recent gains, and this has caused the market to lose direction," the local bank dealer said.
The market had been warily awaiting the Mitsuzuka news conference on the chance that further cautionary comments about the weak yen might emerge, but no such comments were made.
A slew of comments by Japanese officials on Tuesday warning of excessive falls in the yen was still exerting downward pressure on the dollar today.
Against the mark, the dollar was supported near 1.5600 marks, with vague talk of possible bids at this level from some European central banks. Offers were placed near 1.5670 marks.
